name: Casual Friday

lead: Casual Friday lets employees swap business formal clothing for informal outfits on the last day of the work week. Its roots lie in Hawaii's 'Aloha Friday' and early Silicon Valley practice, and it spread widely across US companies in the 1990s.

For appearance, it is a regular occasion where people choose their own clothes at work. Community members discuss it as a test of style: casual does not have to mean an old T-shirt, and some posters describe a go-to look for the day.

paras: People typically keep clothes that fit well, such as clean jeans or chinos with a neat top and shoes, and avoid items that read as sloppy. Company policies differ on what counts as acceptable casual wear.

The practice itself carries no health risk. Social risk is mismatched expectations: workplaces interpret 'casual' differently, and forum posters note that dressing down can be read differently at different offices.

angle.text: Casual Friday gives people a regular workday on which they choose their own clothes. Those who care about style use it to show fit, colour and grooming in a casual setting.

lead: Casual Friday is a workplace tradition that lets employees dress informally on Fridays, in contrast to the business formal dress expected on other days. It is also called dress-down Friday, and in Hawaii 'Aloha Friday'. [1]

It traces to Hawaii's midcentury Aloha Friday custom, which spread to California and then globally, and became known as Casual Friday in the 1990s. In the United States, Hewlett-Packard is described as having let staff dress more casually on Fridays from the 1950s and 1960s. [1] By 1994, 497 of the 1,000 most important US companies reportedly observed it, including General Motors, Ford and IBM. [1]

For people interested in how they look, the day is a recurring chance to present a considered casual style at work; discussions in fitness and style forums mention signature outfits and note that 'dress nice' means different things in different offices. [2][3]
infobox: Hawaii's Aloha Friday; Hewlett-Packard practice in the 1950s-60s [1]

paras: Hawaii's Aloha Friday is the custom from which Casual Friday descends. 'Aloha wear' is regarded in Hawaii as appropriate business attire on any day, and 'Aloha Friday' can simply mean the last working day of the week. [1]

A Grokipedia account describes the Hawaiian Fashion Guild promoting local aloha shirts in the 1960s and lobbying for year-round adoption by 1965. [4] Wikipedia notes the mainland practice began in the 1950s and 1960s with Hewlett-Packard. [1]

The custom became known as Casual Friday in the 1990s, and by 1994 nearly half of the largest US companies observed it. [1] Valerie Steele described its introduction as the most radical change in work fashion since the 1970s. [1]

On T Nation, one poster calls a denim-heavy outfit 'Denim Dan', his casual Friday go-to, while another contrasts an intern's t-shirt, jeans and trainers with an expectation of dressing nicely. [2][3] These are passing mentions rather than a developed doctrine.
